rulings.section: 4. RUN / STOP semantics, the STOP bullet
rulings.currentText: - **STOP** = a **short circuit** across D18 and D19 - a dead short across the motor itself. Not a brake solenoid, not a power cut. "A short circuit may be connected across terminals 18 and 19 (stop) to halt the motor drive." [verified] Book I p.22.
rulings.ruling: ADD. The semantics are correct and stay as written; what is missing is the second, independent source and the clincher, which currently sits in the §3.2 table (condition 5) where it does no argumentative work. Append to the bullet: 'The Maintenance Manual states the same operation independently - "Connect a short circuit across the STOP terminals (D18 and D19): the pointer knob should stop turning" - and then prints the test that rules out every rival reading: "If the pointer knob does not rotate, connect power **momentarily** across the STOP terminals: the knob should turn very rapidly." A brake, a detent or a power-cut input would not spin the motor at full supply when energised. Only a pair of terminals sitting directly across the armature behaves that way, and the same sentence dates the R1 bypass: with power on D18-D19 the dropper is out of circuit, which is why SDC says *momentarily*. [verified] MM p.9.'
rulings.evidence: maintenance-manual.pdf PDF p.11 (printed p.9, folio visible), read as an image at 300 dpi and cross-checked against the text layer. Verbatim: 'Check the motor drive by connecting power to the RUN terminals (D17 and D18). Turn power on. The rotary switch pointer knob should turn. Reverse the power connections: the pointer knob should turn in the opposite direction. Connect a short circuit across the STOP terminals (D18 and D19): the pointer knob should stop turning. If the pointer knob does not rotate, connect power momentarily across the STOP terminals: the knob should turn very rapidly.'

rulings.currentText: **Two unlabelled brass fasteners** sit at the top-left of the decimal block, above and left of the `16`/`ARM` pair. They render as solid heads, not as the dark two-hole jacks used elsewhere, and carry no silkscreen. [verified] that they exist (Photo); [unverified] what they are. Do not model them as terminals.
rulings.ruling: CORRECT twice in one sentence. (a) DELETE 'brass' - write 'Two unlabelled metal fasteners'. The colour is a lighting artefact, not a material reading. (b) CORRECT the position: they are NOT left of the 16/ARM pair. They sit in the upper part of the decimal block, above the 16/ARM hole pair and offset slightly to its RIGHT, roughly over the ARM hole and up-right of it. Suggested replacement: 'Two unlabelled metal fasteners sit in the upper part of the decimal block, above the `16`/`ARM` hole pair and slightly to its right. They render as solid round heads with a struck burr, not as the dark two-hole jacks used elsewhere, and carry no silkscreen. [verified] that they exist and where they are (Commons photographs, both units); [unverified] what they are and what metal. Do not model them as terminals.'
rulings.evidence: raw/photos/commons-minivac601-main.jpg, flat top-down daylight shot, crops at full resolution around x 2980-3340 / y 1380-1720 and x 2800-3300 / y 1240-1700: two solid round heads, silver-white to pale grey, clearly above the ARM hole pair and to its right; the '16' numeral, the two ARM holes and the two heads are all resolvable in the same crop and the heads are the rightmost of the group. raw/photos/commons-minivac601-DSCF1392.jpg (museum unit, tungsten light, oblique) shows the same two heads in the same place rendering warm gold. rulings.section: 2.1 Contact arc versus gap, the paragraph beginning '**0.25 is an unsourced engineering default'
rulings.currentText: **0.25 is an unsourced engineering default, [unverified], not a finding.** It is a sane proportion for a mid-century 16-position non-shorting wafer switch and it produces the right qualitative behaviours, but no manual points at it. Name the constant, comment it as unsourced, and expose it.
rulings.ruling: TIGHTEN. Keep the fallback, the interface, the algorithm, the invariants and the tunable marking exactly as they are - they are right. But the sentence 'It is a sane proportion for a mid-century 16-position non-shorting wafer switch' is the last surviving leg of the refuted argument, and it carries no citation either inside this corpus or outside it. Replace with: 'The appeal to "the classic proportion for a mid-century non-shorting wafer switch" is itself uncited - it appears in the gap finder's file with no source, and the adversarial pass looked for one and found none. Treat 0.25 as an arbitrary tunable chosen because it is a round number strictly inside the only bound the corpus gives (0 < gap < 22.5 degrees) and because it produces the right qualitative behaviours. No source, primary or secondary, points at it. Name the constant, comment it as unsourced, and expose it.'
rulings.evidence: raw/gap-verify-rotary-contact-geometry-and-motor-law.json: R1-R4 refute the finder's three bounding arguments (the SOS run-length reading, the errata's 'almost indistinguishable' note, and the 42 ms square-wave discriminator); D5 withdraws bullets 3, 4 and 6 of the fallback's justification and rules on bullet 5 that it 'carries no citation anywhere in the finder's file and I found none in the corpus'; judgement_on_the_named_fallback: 'is_the_number_defensible: YES as a default, NO as a derivation. ... Keep 0.25. Delete the claim that the manuals point at it.' I re-checked the underlying refutation at source (see RO-05 evidence) and it holds.

rulings.section: 8. Corrections, item 6; and 9. Not settled by the sources, first row ('Angular width of a contact pad vs. the dead gap')
rulings.currentText: §8 item 6 ends: '**No primary source bounds the gap fraction.** [verified] by image-read of the Experiment 18 program table.'  §9 row 1 'What would settle it': 'Under-panel photograph of an original SDC 6473 assembly at measurable resolution; ohmmeter across D16 and one contact while rotating slowly; frame-counted video of an original running the traffic light.'
rulings.ruling: ADD, so the refutation is not read as though it protects 0.25. Append one sentence to §8 item 6: 'The refutation cuts both ways. The adversarial pass records, without asserting it, that if the differential spacing works by latching the mark at one contact's make and holding it until the next contact's make, the printed dash/dot ratio equals pitch / pad_arc = 1/(1 - gap_fraction) - which at 0.25 gives a feeble 1.33 and at 0.5 gives a usable 2.0. On that unresolved reading the SOS program would argue for a *larger* gap than the fallback assumes. Nothing here is a bound in either direction until relays 3-6 are solved.' And ADD a fourth settling route to §9 row 1: 'solving the Experiment 18 relay circuit (relays 3, 4, 5 and 6, with the off-net contacts D4 and D9 sitting at the S/O and O/S boundaries), which would turn the printed dash/dot ratio into a direct bound on pad arc against pitch.'
rulings.evidence: raw/gap-verify-rotary-contact-geometry-and-motor-law.json, refuted.R1 'sting_in_the_tail', and what_would_settle_the_open_parameter item 7: 'Working out the Experiment 18 relay circuit (relays 3, 4, 5, 6). Until that is done, nobody can say whether the SOS program's differential spacing argues for a larger gap, a smaller one, or neither.' I re-verified the netlist the argument rests on from book5-6.pdf PDF p.37 (printed p.31), layout-preserved extraction: the Experiment 18 rotary lines are 6A/D1, 6E/D9, 6G/D4, 6H/D16, 6L/D18, 5E/D19, D1/D2, D2/D3, D3/D6, D6/D7, D7/D8, D8/D11, D11/D12, D12/D13, D16/D17, D17/M+, D18/M-. D3/D6 and D8/D11 bridge across D4/D5 and D9/D10, so D1,D2,D3,D6,D7,D8,D11,D12,D13 are one net and D4, D9 are off it - exactly as §8 item 6(a) already says.

rulings.section: 7. Reference programs for the rotary model (table); and 2. Contact structure
rulings.currentText: The §7 table runs from 'Exp 11, manual rotary' to 'Book VII automatic counter'. Book VII's Experiment 9, the Decimal to Binary Converter, appears nowhere in the file, and neither does the fact that its pulse train is produced by the dead gap.
rulings.ruling: ADD - this is the largest gap this pass found, and it is a late-source gap. Add a §7 row: '| Exp 9, decimal-to-binary counting converter | Book VII p.24 (601/6010 joint manual) | `D0/D19`, `D1/D2`, `D2/D3`, `D3/D4`, `D4/D5`, `D5/D6`, `D6/D7`, `D7/D8`, `D8/D9`, `D9/D10`, `D10/D11`, `D11/D12`, `D12/D13`, `D13/D14`, `D14/D15`, `D16/M+`, `D16/D18`, `D17/M-`, `(D18/Ω33)(Ω33/D19)`, plus `6C/D1`, `(6C/Ω150)(Ω150/6E)`, `6F/6-`. D1 through D15 strapped into ONE net; D0 kept off it and tied to D19 as the stop; the wiper at M+ and also at D18. |' And add a paragraph to §2, after the break-before-make paragraph: '**The dead gap is the pulse source, and a shipped program depends on it.** Book VII Experiment 9 straps D1-D15 into a single net and feeds relay 6 from it through the wiper. SDC: "Connections are then made from the rotary switch through relay 6 to the counter. As the rotary switch turns, it makes contact with the terminals and produces pulses which operates the counter," and "The rotary switch returns to zero, sending a pulse to the counter as it passes each rotary switch terminal." With all fifteen contacts on one net there is no other edge available: every pulse is a break at an inter-contact gap followed by the next make. A model with no dead gap, or with a gap the relay model cannot resolve at running speed, silently produces one pulse instead of n and the converter reads zero. [verified] Book VII pp.24-25, image-read.'
rulings.evidence: book7-capacitor-resistor.pdf PDF p.29 (printed folio 24, visible) at 200 dpi, read as an image - the full Experiment 9 program, four columns, with the fourth column carrying D0/D19 and the fourteen D-to-D straps D1/D2 through D14/D15, then D16/M+, D16/D18, D17/M-, and the braced pair (D18/Ω33)(Ω33/D19). The same page carries the prose 'The first five sections of the MINIVAC are programmed as a binary counter (8421 code). Connections are then made from the rotary switch through relay 6 to the counter. As the rotary switch turns, it makes contact with the terminals and produces pulses which operates the counter.' book7 PDF p.30 (printed folio 25) at 200 dpi carries the procedure: '1. Set the rotary switch dial to any number from 0 through 15. 2. Turn power on. The rotary switch returns to zero, sending a pulse to the counter as it passes each rotary switch terminal.' Page offset confirmed independently on three folios (PDF 26 = 21, PDF 29 = 24, PDF 30 = 25, PDF 31 = 26).

rulings.section: 6.1 The eight idioms, 'Ring with one break' row
rulings.currentText: | **Ring with one break** | Strap all sixteen contacts into a chain and encode a number by *removing* one strap: "to enter 5, remove D5/D6." | [likely] - Book VII pp.22-24, OCR degraded, not image-verified |
rulings.ruling: CORRECT on three counts and UPGRADE the tag. (a) It is not all sixteen contacts: the chain is D1 through D15, fourteen straps. D0 is deliberately off the chain and wired `D0/D19` as the stop. (b) The pages are wrong: the chain program is Book VII printed p.24, the idiom is stated on printed p.25 (multiplication), p.26 (division) and p.29 (the summary), not pp.22-24. (c) [likely] becomes [verified] - all four pages were image-read in this pass. Suggested replacement cell: 'Strap D1-D15 into one chain (D0 stays off it, tied to `D0/D19` as the stop) and encode a number by *removing* one strap, which splits the ring so the wiper only reaches the sub-chain below the break: "if the divisor is 7, remove D7/D8"; "Enter 5 (00101) on the rotary switch by removing D5/D6." The programmed effect is a rotary switch that emits *n* pulses per revolution instead of sixteen. | [verified] Book VII printed p.24 (chain), pp.25, 26 and 29 (the idiom), image-read. Book VII is the joint 601/6010 manual; the idiom uses only 601 D-terminals. |'
rulings.evidence: book7-capacitor-resistor.pdf PDF p.31 (printed folio 26, visible), 200 dpi image read, three occurrences on the one page: 'Set the rotary switch to 6. / Remove D6/D7.'; 'The divisor is now entered on the rotary switch by removing the connection from the divisor's digit to the next higher digit. (For example, if the divisor is 7, remove D7/D8.)'; 'Enter 5 (00101) on the rotary switch by removing D5/D6.' PDF p.30 (printed 25) carries the same instruction for multiplication: 'Remove the connection on the rotary switch from the number which has been entered to the next higher number. (For example, if 7 has been entered, remove the connection D7/D8.)' PDF p.34 (printed 29 by the established offset) repeats '(For example, to enter 5, remove D5/D6.)' and '(For example, to enter 8 remove D8/D9.)'. The chain itself, D1/D2 through D14/D15 with D0 excluded, is on PDF p.29 (printed 24) - see RO-06.

rulings.section: 3.2 The documented drive conditions, row 6 and the paragraph beneath it
rulings.currentText: | 6 | Resistance across STOP | 15, 22 or 33 Ω across D18-D19 | Shunts the motor; slows it continuously. | [verified] Book VII p.21 |  ... 'Condition 6 is the one most implementations get wrong. Book VII p.21 ships an optional program connection written as the braced pair `(D18/Ω)(Ω/D19)` with the footnote, image-verified: ...'
rulings.ruling: STRENGTHEN. The paragraph presents the shunt as an optional extra in one program. It is also a *required* element of another. Append: 'It is not always optional. Book VII printed p.24, the decimal-to-binary counting converter, wires `(D18/Ω33)(Ω33/D19)` as an ordinary program line with no asterisk and no optional footnote - a 33 Ω resistor permanently across STOP for the whole run. So the D18-D19 net must accept an arbitrary resistance as a first-class wiring case, not as a special mode; and a fixture generator that treats every braced Ω pair as optional will drop a wire this program needs.'
rulings.evidence: book7-capacitor-resistor.pdf PDF p.29 (printed p.24) at 200 dpi: the fourth program column ends '(D18/Ω33)(Ω33/D19)' with no asterisk anywhere on the page and no optional footnote, in contrast with PDF p.26 (printed p.21) where the same shape is printed '(D18/Ω)(Ω/D19)*' with '* Optional' below the table and the fuller footnote '* This is an optional connection. Use a 15, 22 or 33 ohm resistor to decrease the speed of the motor.' Both pages read as images in this pass.

rulings.section: 6.1 The eight idioms, 'Seek and stop' row
rulings.currentText: | **Seek and stop** | Tie the wiper to a STOP terminal (`D16/D19`) and drive the target contact to whatever potential D18 sits at. Arrival shorts D18-D19 through the arm and the motor halts on the target. | [verified] Books II-IV p.15 Exp 7 |
rulings.ruling: CORRECT the example wire or the citation - as written they do not match. Books II-IV p.15, Experiment 7 wires the mirror image: `D18/D16` puts the wiper on **D18**, and the daisy-chained slide-switch poles feed the target through `6S/D19`. The `D16/D19` form is real but comes from other programs (Exp 12 p.85, the two-bit adder p.87, Book I Answer 18 p.32, the three-floor elevator p.11). Suggested cell: 'Tie the wiper to one STOP terminal and drive the target contact to the other. Arrival shorts D18-D19 through the arm and the motor halts on the target. Both polarities are shipped: `D16/D19` with the target on the D18 side (Exp 12, two-bit adder, Answer 18), and `D18/D16` with the target chain on `D19` (Exp 7). | [verified] Books II-IV p.15 Exp 7; Books II-IV p.85 Exp 12 |'

There is no D16/D19 line. Contrast PDF p.91 (printed 85), Experiment 12: '... 6X/D17, D16/D19, D18/M-'; and PDF p.93 (printed 87), two-bit adder: 'D16/D19, D17/M+, D18/M-'.

rulings.currentText: §7: '| Answer 18, stop at zero | Book I p.32 | `6+/6Y`, `6X/D17`, `M-/D18`, `5Z/D18`, `5Y/D0`, `D16/D19`. Seek-and-stop on a single contact via a normally-closed pushbutton pair. |' - with no mention of the errata note that governs the program.
rulings.ruling: ADD. The wire list and page are exactly right; what is missing is the factory errata note, which is in programs.md as ER-03 but nowhere in rotary.md. Append to the §7 cell, and reference it from §1's 'Position 0 is not a home position' paragraph: 'Errata, notes to Book I p.28: "Problem 18: Note that pushbutton 5 is used to keep the rotary switch from stopping at D0 when pushbutton 6 is being held down." Holding pushbutton 5 breaks its normally-closed pair, lifting D0 out of the stop net - the documented way to run past position 0. Further evidence that D0 is an ordinary contact with no special hardware behaviour: its stop behaviour is created and removed by ordinary program wiring. [verified] Errata, Book I p.28.'
rulings.evidence: errata.pdf / errata.txt, BOOK I block, verbatim: 'page 28: Problem 7: Note that light 1 and relay 1 should both be on only if both pushbutton 1 and pushbutton 2 are DOWN. / Problem 18: Note that pushbutton 5 is used to keep the rotary switch from stopping at DO when pushbutton 6 is being held down.' Answer 18 itself confirmed from book1.pdf PDF p.34 (printed p.32) layout extraction: 6+/6Y, 6X/D17, M-/D18, 5Z/D18, 5Y/D0, D16/D19. The note is already carried in docs/research/programs.md as ER-03, so this is a cross-file omission, not a new finding.

rulings.currentText: The Automobile Speed Timer computes 83.52 mph for one revolution during the run, then divides: 83.52 / 2 = 41.76 for two revolutions, 83.52 / 3 = 27.64 for three.
rulings.ruling: ADD a bracket so nobody 'fixes' the transcription or encodes the wrong number in a fixture: '... 83.52 / 3 = 27.64 for three (SDC's own arithmetic slip - 83.52 / 3 is 27.84; the page really prints 27.64, image-verified at 400 dpi, so it is not OCR damage, and the factory errata sheet does not correct it).' The argument the file draws from the division - that dividing by revolution count presupposes constant angular velocity - is unaffected.
rulings.evidence: book5-6.pdf PDF p.13 (printed p.7) rendered at 400 dpi, quotient region cropped and enlarged: '83.52 / 2 = 41.76 miles per hour.' and '83.52 / 3 = 27.64 miles per hour.' Both sets of glyphs are clean, same typeface, no scan damage; the 6 and the 4 are unambiguous. The corpus already carries one uncorrected SDC misprint of this kind (the '(1 to 19)' terminal range, §8 correction 2); this is a second.

confirmedCorrect: 3.1 Internal topology, re-verified independently in this pass and confirmed exactly as the file states it: R1 between D17 and D19; the motor between D18 and D19; R2 between D18 and D19 in parallel with the motor; D19 the mid-node. Maintenance Manual printed p.9 (PDF p.11) at 300 dpi - the D17 rail runs right and down through the right-hand zigzag to the bottom rail labelled D19; the D18 rail runs right and down through the middle zigzag to the same bottom rail; the motor circle sits on its own stub between the D18 and D19 rails; one 'RESISTORS' leader points at both zigzags. Book I printed p.22 (PDF p.24) at 300 dpi - identical network, terminals labelled 17, 18, 19 with RUN and STOP annotations. Two independent drawings, no discrepancy. Critic C2 and C5 are both correctly resolved in the file.

4. STOP is a dead short across the motor, not a brake, not a detent, not a power cut. Book I printed p.22 verbatim: 'Power must be supplied to terminals 17 and 18 (run) to operate the motor drive. A short circuit may be connected across terminals 18 and 19 (stop) to halt the motor drive.' Book I printed p.23 verbatim: 'The motor stops when pushbutton 6 is pushed because a short circuit is created across the STOP terminals (D18 and D19). Current flows through pushbutton 6 instead of through the motor.' Both image-read. The file's 'STOP wins over RUN through the shared terminal 18' and the two-stopping-mechanisms reading of Experiment 12 step 5 ('this time because power is no longer connected to the motor circuit') are both exact. Only the MM clincher is missing - see RO-01.

4. 'R1 is what makes the short safe', including the ruling that SDC's plural 'resistors' in 'The resistors make it possible to connect a short circuit across the STOP terminals ... without over-loading the power supply' is loose prose because R2 is shorted out by the very short it is credited with surviving. Verified verbatim from Book I printed p.22 at 300 dpi, and the electrical reasoning follows from the image-verified topology.

2. No detents, ratchet, index spring or click stop, tagged [likely] as an argument from silence. The supporting structure is right: a detented switch cannot produce the errata's documented rest-between-contacts hang, and the Maintenance Manual spare-parts list names only 6471 Motor, 6472 Drive Wheel Assembly and 6473 Complete Rotary Switch Assembly (verified verbatim from the printed p.11 parts table). Nothing in the Commons photographs contradicts it. Keeping this at [likely] rather than [verified] is the right call.

2. The dead gap as a documented program hang. Errata, notes to Book V page 11, verified verbatim: 'Note: It is possible for the "elevator" to get stuck at a floor. This happens when the pointer knob stops between adjacent terminals - for example, between D6 and D7 - and is not making proper connection with either. In such case, move the pointer knob so that it is pointing directly at one of the terminals.' And the Experiment 9 program does contain D6/D7 - verified from book5-6.pdf printed p.11, which prints D0/D1, D6/D7 and D12/D13 together with the floor table 'Floor 1 D0-D1 / Floor 2 D6-D7 / Floor 3 D12-D13'. The file's inference - that the wiper can rest between two electrically identical contacts and connect to neither - is exactly right.

1. Contact pitch 22.5 degrees, sixteen equal positions, [verified]. book5-6.pdf printed p.7 verbatim: 'Since the program above indicates a revolution of the rotary switch when the dial has completed 15/16 of a revolution, we must multiply the number of complete revolutions in a minute by 16/15 to obtain a "revolutions per minute" figure for the dial plate.' Corroborated visually by the sixteen equal silkscreened sectors in commons-minivac601-DSCF1392.jpg.

1. Rotation sense: increasing dial numbers run clockwise as the operator sees them (15-0-1 across the top, 2-3-4-5-6 down the right, 7-8-9 across the bottom, 10-11-12-13-14 up the left), verified from the unobstructed Commons crop; Book I printed p.20's VIEW UNDER PANEL figure is mirrored (0 at top, 1 at about 11 o'clock, 8 at the bottom, 15 at about 1 o'clock) and is a drafting convention, verified by image read; and Books V-VI p.56's 'counterclockwise (towards 9) ... clockwise (towards 7)' genuinely contradicts the panel, verified verbatim. The file's refusal to resolve the discrepancy, and its instruction never to take rotation sense from Book VI, match critic C13's action exactly.

1. Twenty terminals, forty holes: sixteen hole-pairs in the ring, four in the left-hand column, D18 shared by the RUN and STOP brackets. Verified in the unobstructed DSCF1392 crop, where the brackets and all four column labels (16/ARM, 17, 18, 19) are legible.

8, correction 2. Book I printed p.20 literally prints '8 = terminal number (1 to 19) . . . for example D8'. Verified at 300 dpi; the glyphs are clean and it is not an OCR mangling of a placeholder. The substantive point - the printed range wrongly omits D0, which exists and is used, while MM printed p.10 gives it correctly as 'D0 through D15' - stands. Matches critic C15.

8, correction 6(a). Experiment 18's D3/D6 and D8/D11 bridge across D4/D5 and D9/D10, merging D1, D2, D3, D6, D7, D8, D11, D12, D13 into one nine-contact mark net for nine Morse elements, so no run-length argument exists and the dot/dash difference must come from relays 3-6. Re-read from the layout-preserved program table on book5-6.pdf printed p.31 and independently confirmed against the adversarial verifier's 450 dpi read. The conclusion 'No primary source bounds the gap fraction' is correct - see RO-05 for the one thing worth adding.

2.1 The core gap ruling. Pitch [verified]; the arc/gap split given nowhere in Books I-VII, the Maintenance Manual or the errata; the corpus bounding it only as 0 < gap < 22.5 degrees; the under-panel figure being schematic (I re-read it at 300 dpi - a plain circle, sixteen closely-spaced dot pairs, a hatched wiper bar with a rectangular tip and a double-headed rotation arrow, no pad arcs, no dimensions); the Experiment 11 step 4 back-and-forth observation as the primary demonstration that the gap is visible to the naked eye ([verified] that the observation is prescribed, [unverified] any number from it); and the point-wiper / finite-wiper equivalence argument (break-before-make holds iff wiper width < gap width, ON window = c + w). All correct and all honestly tagged.

2. Break-before-make, verified verbatim from Book I printed p.21: 'Notice that light 5 goes OFF before light 6 comes ON. This shows that the rotary switch is designed to disconnect the arm from one contact before making connection with the next contact. The switch operation is described as "break-before-make" ...' - together with the file's consequence that contact_at must be able to return no contact and can never return two.

2. Sweep semantics, 'every contact the wiper crosses fires', and the no-jump rule. Book I printed p.22 verbatim: 'The rotary switch connections are made sequentially whether the pointer is turned by hand or driven by the motor.' Combination Lock corroboration verified at source: Books V-VI printed p.52 footnote '* This last connection is optional; it will cause the machine to indicate an error if 8 is passed at any point.' and printed p.53 'you must not include any connection which will touch off a connection further along.' The Combination Lock's only rotary wire is D16/M+ with no D17/D18/D19, so the sequential rule does bind hand motion - correct as stated.

2. Contact materials and bearing, verified verbatim from MM printed p.2 including SDC's own misspelling: 'To provide low contact resistance, the rotary switch uses silver-plated circuits. The rotary switch contact fingers are made of berryllium copper; the drive shaft is made of stainless steel running in an oil-impregnated bronze bearing.'

2. Knob-to-wiper alignment as a loose per-unit quantity, and the wiper_offset_deg recommendation. MM printed p.2 verified verbatim: 'Replace the pointer knob and realign it by connecting a light through one of the switch contacts on the rotary switch dial. Adjust the position of the knob on the shaft so the light comes on when the knob is pointing at the connected switch position.' MM printed p.10 verified: 'Check the knob alignment to be sure that the knob has not turned on the drive shaft.'

3. Supply and motor context, all verified verbatim from MM printed p.2: 'The power supply is rated at 1.5 amps continuous with a nominal 12 volts output. All switches are rated at 3 amps; relay contacts are rated in excess of 3 amps.' and 'The drive motor is operated at less than one-third rated voltage.' Plus MM printed p.4 step 3, 'The unloaded power supply outlet voltage should be approximately 13 volts', and the resettable circuit breaker at step 2. The file's caution that 'less than one-third rated voltage' refers to the motor's unknown rating, so the ~3x fast_rpm estimate collapses if the motor is not a 12 V unit, is exactly right.

3. The friction drive and its repair step, verified verbatim from MM printed p.10 step 5: 'To assure proper friction drive, adjust the motor bracket and spring the motor shaft against the edge of the drive wheel.' The file's caution that 'spring' is a verb there and that no spring appears in the parts list is correct, and its [likely] tag on the permanently-engaged, clutchless drive is the right level.

3.2 conditions 3, 4, 5 and 7, and the R1-and-R2-are-power-resistors note. MM printed p.10 step 3 verified verbatim: 'Check each of the two resistors by connecting power across them. The resistors should heat up in about 20 seconds. If a resistor does not heat up, it is defective.' Values never given anywhere - confirmed by whole-document reading of the Maintenance Manual.

3.3 Braking and coast. The premise is correctly split from the magnitudes: R2 sitting permanently across the armature is [verified] from the two schematics, so even a de-energised stop is a braked stop; and coast angle, spin-down and reversal time are correctly left [unverified] with two separately-named parameters. The observation that coast, overrun, momentum and inertia appear nowhere in the corpus holds against the extracted text layers I searched. The four-way argument for and against coast, including the point that the errata's example is floor 2 (D6-D7), a landing reachable only under motor drive, while floor 1 (D0-D1) is the one an operator parks by hand, is supported: Books V-VI printed p.12 does say 'Set the "elevator" at the first floor by setting the pointer knob at D0.'

3.4 Speed. 'No speed is specified anywhere' and the instruction to measure your own unit are verified verbatim from Books V-VI printed p.7. The 45 rpm figure is correctly labelled an example assumption. The '48 is not a dial speed' trap is exactly right: the page multiplies the physical 45 rpm by 16/15 to get 48 because the program's count fires at D15, 15/16 of the way round - I confirmed the mechanism independently from the Speed Timer program on printed p.6, where 5C/D15 puts relay 5's coil on D15. The 'more than a second from zero to nine' refutation is right: that passage compares two human operations, not motor speeds.

3.4 Constant angular velocity as SDC's own working assumption, [verified] from the Speed Timer's division by revolution count on printed p.7. The caveat that this is not a claim about instantaneous spin-up is correct. (One arithmetic wrinkle - see RO-18.)

4. The net-model prerequisite. Both errata general notes verified verbatim: 'All + and - terminals are connected together. For example, a connection to 1+ is the same as a connection to 3+, 6+, or M+. Similarly, a connection to 2- is the same as a connection to 4-, 5-, or M-.' and 'In addition to those terminals specifically marked "common," common terminals are any set of terminals which are interconnected: for instance, the two terminals at 6R, the six at M10, or the four at 3com.' The file's use of the second rule to license D-contact strapping chains is right. Matches critic C4.
4. Answer 14 (`5+/5Y`, `5Z/6X`, `6Y/D17`, `M-/D18`) and Answer 15 (`6+/6X`, `6Y/D17`, `M-/D18`, `D18/5X`, `5Y/D19`) - both exact, both on Book I printed p.31, and both correctly described.

5. Manual operation. All four bullets check out at source except the shift-register page (RO-13): the friction-drive slip instruction ('slow the rotary switch down by holding the pointer knob back during one revolution', Errata notes to Book V page 31), the direction-matters instructions ('always turn the pointer knob clockwise when indicating a letter for coding', Errata notes to Book V page 33; 'Turn the rotary switch clockwise until the pointer knob is pointing at the letter you wish to code', Books V-VI p.34), and the general errata note 'try carrying out the procedure slowly; some programs are not designed for high-speed operation' - all verified verbatim.

6. The dial as decimal I/O and as storage. Both Books II-IV quotes verified verbatim on printed p.3: 'The rotary switch remains in a particular position until it is moved and thus enables MINIVAC 601 to "remember" a decimal number' and 'When operated with the motor, the rotary switch becomes an output device, since the motor may be controlled by the processing unit of the MINIVAC 601 and caused to stop with the pointer indicating the number which is to be communicated as output information.' The range quote is verified on printed p.5: 'The decimal input capabilities of the MINIVAC 601 are limited to the numbers from zero through fifteen.' The observation that the manuals never use 'hexadecimal' holds.

6.1 The idiom rows for Range detect, Seek one of two, Relay as brake, Wiper as rail and Arithmetic offset. Verified at source: the traffic light's adjacent-run straps; Experiment 8's two-floor elevator on printed p.11 (6N/D18, 6Y/D1, D1/M+, D7/M-, D16/D19, 6J/D17 - two targets at opposite rails with the wiper on D19, exactly as described, mechanism correctly tagged [likely]); the Reaction Time Tester on printed p.60 (4K/D19, 4L/4-, D18/M-, D16/D17 - both the relay-as-brake and the wiper-as-rail wires exactly as quoted); the CQ transmitter's D16/D17 on printed p.30; and the Match Game's offset-3 straps D1/D4, D2/D5 ... D12/D15 on printed p.55.

6.2 The metronome. The 17-wire program on Books V-VI printed p.4 matches the file's code block exactly, wire for wire (4R/D3, 4S/5R, 4T/D5, 4U/D7, 4V/5T, 4W/D9, 5S/6K, 6C/6L, 6E/D16, 6F/6-, 6G/D1, 6G/6N, 6H/D17, 6J/6K, 6J/6+, 6L/D18, 6N/6-). The 'to use' quote is verbatim. SDC's 'only four periods can be produced ... capable of generating 15 different periods' is verbatim. The file's refusal to assert a 2:4:6:8 period ratio - asserting only strictly increasing periods, on the ground that a reversing drive's half-period includes acceleration and deceleration - is correct and matches the adversarial pass's D2.

6.2 'The metronome's tick is not a fixed frequency' and the warning that an integer-with-instant-reversal model produces a degenerate metronome. Sound, and it is the right consequence to draw from the drive-condition table.

7. Experiment 12's wire list (`6+/5Y`, `5X/D17`, `6-/D18`, `6-/6Y`, `6X/D19`) exact against Book I printed p.23. Experiment 14's list exact against Book I printed p.24, and the file is right that the errata's 'change 6Y to 6V' corrects the *diagram* - the printed program already reads 6V/D17. Experiment 7's rotary lines exact against Books II-IV printed p.15. Experiment 12 (binary-to-decimal) and the two-bit adder exact against Books II-IV printed pp.85 and 87, including the quote 'each combination of switches energizes one and only one terminal of the rotary switch'. The Book VII automatic counter's six rotary lines exact against Book VII printed p.21.

7. Landing-pad design, and both required regression cases. Experiment 9's two-contact pads (D0/D1, D6/D7, D12/D13) and the floor table are verified from Books V-VI printed p.11; the errata variant the test must name (base corrections 4G/4H -> 4G/5H and D16/M- -> D16/M+, versus the optional reliability variant) is correctly attributed to Experiment 9 and not Experiment 8, matching critic C9 and §8 correction 3, which I re-checked against the printed Experiment 8 program (it contains 5F/6X and 6C/6G, not 5F/6C and 6C/6-).

8, correction 8. Transcription counts confirmed: the Automobile Speed Timer on Books V-VI printed p.6 has 35 wires (nine rows of four, less one in the short final row), and 6C/6G is indeed the last entry in the third column where it is easy to lose; the Morse encoder on printed p.33 has 17 decimal-side wires including 2F/D15, 3G/D8, 4F/D14, 5com/D2 and 6F/D3.

10. The Gardi replica section. The consequences drawn are strict and correct - detents, reed switches and a solenoid clutch are his design, not the 601's, and the Hackaday contamination warning is well aimed. Nothing in the late sources changes it.
nothing_further_open: Of the rotary-relevant cross-file contradictions in raw/critic-completeness.json, C2 (two resistors), C4 (single +/- rails), C5 (whether MM p.9 had been read), C9 (the errata block belongs to Experiment 9), C13 (rotation sense, primary sources conflict, do not resolve) and C15 (the '1 to 19' misprint) are all already correctly resolved inside rotary.md. C10 (Book VII scope) is the only one leaving a residue, addressed by RO-09. No new cross-file contradiction was found in this pass.
